questions.q: Iodobenzene is heated at about 200 °C with an excess of copper powder. The organic product is:
questions.explain: The Ullmann reaction joins two aryl groups through a new C–C bond: 2 C₆H₅I + 2 Cu → C₆H₅–C₆H₅ + 2 CuI. Diaryl ethers come from the separate Ullmann-type reaction of aryl halides with phenoxides.

questions.q: Which aryl halide does NOT undergo the classical Ullmann reaction with Cu on heating?
questions.explain: Plain chlorobenzene has a strong C–Cl bond and an electron-rich ring, so copper does not react with it. A nitro group ortho or para to Cl makes the aryl chloride electron-poor enough to couple, and iodides react most easily.

questions.q: According to the accepted mechanism, the classical Ullmann reaction proceeds through:
questions.explain: Copper first gives an arylcopper species, Ar–Cu, which reacts with a second Ar–X to form Ar–Ar and CuX. Electron spin resonance studies rule out free radicals, which is the trap if you mix it up with the Fittig reaction.

questions.q: The compound shown is heated with copper-bronze. The product is:
questions.explain: The ortho nitro group activates the C–Cl bond, and the two aryl groups join where the chlorine atoms were, so each NO₂ stays ortho to the new biaryl bond. 4,4′-Dinitrobiphenyl would come from 4-chloronitrobenzene.
